Absence of the combined rod-and-cone response on electroretinogram.

A type of rigidity in which a muscle responds with cogwheellike jerks to the use of constant force in bending the limb (i.e., it gives way in little, repeated jerks when the muscle is passively stretched).
Focal proliferation of glial cells in the basal ganglia.
Nystagmus consisting of horizontal to-and-fro eye movements of equal velocity.

Thickening of the peribronchovascular interstitium, a connective tissue sheath that surrounds the central bronchi and pulmonary arteries. The peribronchovascular interstitium extends from the level of the pulmonary hila into the peripheral lung. This feature may be ascertained on high-resolution computer tomography.
Broadening of the soft tissues (non-edematous swelling of soft tissues) of the digital tips in all dimensions associated with an increased longitudinal and lateral curvature of the nails.

Expectoration (coughing up) of a broncholith. Broncholithiasis is defined as the presence of calculi in the tracheobronchial tree. It is a rare disease but can be characterized by clinical and radiological findings of a calcified lymph node eroding bronchial wall and opening into the bronchial lumen.

Polypoidal masses arising mainly from the mucous membranes of the nose and paranasal sinuses. They are freely movable and nontender overgrowths of the mucosa that frequently accompany allergic rhinitis.
Chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa.
Collapse of part of a lung associated with absence of inflation (air) of that part.
Abnormal appearance of material expectorated (coughed up) from the respiratory system and that is composed of mucus but may contain other substances such as pus, blood, microorganisms, and fibrin.

A developmental defect characterized by abnormal connection of one or more pulmonary veins to the superior or inferior vena cava, the right atrium, or the coronary sinus, resulting in a left-to-right shunt of oxygenated blood.
Chronic inflammation of the bronchi.
Common atrium without defining morphologic features.
Abnormality of the spatial relationship of the atria to other components of the heart.
A high-pitched whistling sound associated with labored breathing.
An abnormality of the pulmonary situs, i.e., of the sidedness of the morphological right and left lungs, in which the morphology of both left and right lungs is the same.
Any structural anomaly of the principal vein draining blood from the lower portion of the body.

Complete absence of the dynein arms of respiratory motile cilia, that is, absence of the inner and the outer dynein arms, which normally are situated inside and outside of the peripheral microtubules of motile cilia. This feature is usually appreciated by electron microscopy.
A deviation from the normally well coordinated pattern of intracellular and intercellular synchrony of motile cilia. Dyskinetic cilia usually beat out of synchrony relative to neighboring cilia.
An anomaly of the mobility of ejaculated sperm.
Inflammation of the nasal mucosa with nasal congestion.
Obstruction of conducting airways of the lung.
A chronic form of sinusitis.
Polysplenia is a congenital disease manifested by multiple small accessory spleens.
Increased susceptibility to mycobacterial infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of mycobacterial infection.

The patient stands with the feet placed together and balance and is asked to close his or her eyes. A loss of balance upon eye closure is a positive Romberg sign and is interpreted as indicating a deficit in proprioception.
An increased concentration of sedoheptulose in the urine. Sedoheptulose is a monosaccharide with seven carbon atoms and a ketone functional group.
Greater than normal amounts of fat in the feces. This is a result of malabsorption of lipids in the small intestine and results in frothy foul-smelling fecal matter that floats.
An abnormality of the renal tubules.
Impairment of bile flow due to obstruction in bile ducts.
Inflammation of the liver.
An increased concentration of glucose in the blood following a meal.
A type of anemia characterized by an abnormally low concentration of hemoglobin in the erythrocytes and lower than normal size of the erythrocytes.
An abnormality of myelination of nerves in the central nervous system.
Respiratory failure in the newborn.

In newborns, the two frontal bones, two parietal bones, and one occipital bone are joined by fibrous sutures, which form a small posterior fontanelle, and a larger, diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle. These regions allow for the skull to pass the birth canal and for later growth. The fontanelles gradually ossify, whereby the posterior fontanelle usually closes by eight weeks and the anterior fontanelle by the 9th to 16th month of age. Large fontanelles are diagnosed if the fontanelles are larger than age-dependent norms.
A separation of the rectus abdominis muscle into right and left halves (which are normally joined at the midline at the linea alba).
A position of the fetus at delivery in which the fetus enters the birth canal with the buttocks or feet first.
Reduced depth of the orbits associated with prominent-appearing ocular globes.
Severe reduction of the ability to see defined as visual acuity less than 6/60 (20/200 in US notation; 0.1 in decimal notation) but at least 3/60 (20/400 in US notation; 0.05 in decimal notation).
Absence or underdevelopment of the vermis of cerebellum.
A morphological abnormality of the optic disc, i.e., of the portion of the optic nerve clinically visible on fundoscopic examination.
Any anomaly of the pigmentation of the fundus, the posterior part of the eye including the retina and optic nerve.
Longitudinal densities on radiographs located in a metaphysis (the narrow region of a long bone between the epiphysis and the diaphysis).

Mottling (spots or blotches with different shades) of the retinal pigment epithelium, i.e., localized or generalized fundal pigment granularity associated with processes at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium.
Inflammation of the lip.

A rash composed of pustular lesions. A pustule is defined as a vesicle or bulla containing purulent material. It varies in size and may occur at different levels within the epidermis: subcorneal, intraepidermal, or basement membrane zones. The pustules may or may not be sterile and are normally filled with neutrophils.
An abnormality of the lip.
Any structural abnormality of the vagina.
An abnormality of the mouth.
A circumscribed area of pus or necrotic debris in the skin.
Recurrent or persistent superficial Candida infections of the skin, mucous membranes, and nails.
Increased susceptibility to Staphylococcus aureus infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of Staphylococcus aureus infection.
An anomaly of the toenail.
A circumscribed, solid elevation of skin with no visible fluid, varying in size from a pinhead to less than 10mm in diameter at the widest point.
Inflammatory cells within the wall and ostia of the hair follicle, creating a follicular-based pustule.
A small elevation of the skin containing cloudy or purulent material usually consisting of necrotic inflammatory cells.
Redness of the skin, caused by hyperemia of the capillaries in the lower layers of the skin.

Chronic accumulation and overgrowth of the fungus Candida albicans on the mucous membranes of the mouth, generally manifested as associated with creamy white lesions on the tongue or inner cheeks, occasionally spreading to the gums, tonsils, palate or oropharynx.
Increased susceptibility to cutaneous fungal infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of cutaneous fungal infections.
An abnormality of the endocardium.
An abnormality of temperature homeostasis.
Any anomaly of lymphocyte function.
Infections of the skin that happen multiple times.
